definition.text: Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish, the trash or garbage of items thrown away by the public.

facts.text: Its make-up varies greatly between places and over time; where recycling is well developed, what is left is mainly plastic film and non-recyclable packaging.
Most definitions leave out industrial, agricultural, medical and radioactive waste and sewage sludge.
Typical Chinese municipal waste is 55.9% food residue, 11.2% plastics and 8.5% paper.
The industry has four parts: recycling, composting, disposal and waste-to-energy incineration.
Waste hierarchies rank methods from most to least preferred: reduce and reuse, recycle or compost, recover energy, then treat and dispose.
It produces large amounts of methane, nearly 90% of which could be avoided with existing technologies.

title: Source separation of waste
article: Municipal solid waste#Waste handling and separation, storage and processing at the source

definition.text: Source separation means sorting waste into types, such as biodegradable, recyclable, residual and hazardous, where it is produced.

facts.text: It improves recycling, prevents contamination, allows composting and ensures hazardous waste is properly treated.
Separated and mixed wastes are processed at materials recovery facilities using hand sorting, screens, magnets and optical sorting.
Segregation, composting and recycling can cut methane emissions from municipal waste.

definition.text: Reuse means using items again, by repairing, gifting, refurbishing or lending them, instead of throwing them away.

facts.text: Reuse lengthens product life and reduces the need for fresh raw materials.
Online networks such as Freecycle list unwanted items for others to reuse, reducing landfill pollution.

definition.text: Waste-to-energy is the generation of power from municipal waste, by burning it or by capturing landfill gas, pyrolysis or gasification.

facts.text: Older incinerators emitted many pollutants, but new rules and technology have greatly reduced this.
US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels and mercury by over 90%.
Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as bioenergy.

definition.text: Particulate matter is microscopic solid or liquid particles suspended in the air.

facts.text: Particles mixed with air are called an aerosol; they come from both natural and human sources.
Major components include wind-blown mineral dust, sea salt, organic matter and particles formed from gases such as SO2 and ammonia.
It is considered the most dangerous air pollution because particles reach deep into the lungs and travel in the blood to organs such as the brain.
There is no safe level of exposure, and airborne particulate matter is a Group 1 carcinogen.
Fine particles (PM2.5) are the leading environmental risk factor for early death worldwide.
Because many sources are human, it is a risk that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it.
After the US Clean Air Act of 1970, combined emissions of criteria and precursor pollutants fell 79% from 1970 to 2024.

definition.text: Particles are grouped by diameter: coarse PM10 (10 micrometres or less), fine PM2.5 (2.5 micrometres or less) and ultrafine particles.

facts.text: Size is a key factor in how much harm a particle can do.
Coarse PM10 particles lodge in the nose, throat and upper airways.
Fine PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the smallest airways and air sacs.
Across all causes of death, PM2.5 has more severe effects than PM10.

title: Health effects of particulate matter

definition.text: Breathing particulate matter is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths.

facts.text: It contributes to stroke, heart disease, respiratory disease, many cancers and preterm birth, and to cognitive impairment.
Worldwide, PM2.5 exposure contributed to 7.9 million deaths in 2023: 4.9 million linked to outdoor and 2.8 million to household air pollution.
The link between particle pollution and premature deaths was first shown in the early 1970s; the 1993 Harvard Six Cities study established it firmly for cities.
Both short-term and long-term exposure cause harm.
In the EU, PM2.5 deaths fell 57% between 2005 and 2023, attributed to policies that cut primary PM2.5 emissions by 38%.
China's 2013 air pollution action plan cut annual average PM2.5 by a third by 2017, with fewer deaths.

notes: Death counts differ by study and year: the 2021 Global Burden of Disease gives 7.83 million deaths from outdoor PM2.5 (S:da0132b18423), while the 2023 figure gives 4.9 million outdoor; Air pollution page gives 4.7 million (S:20b96110021e). Not treated as conflicts because sources and years differ.

definition.text: The World Health Organization sets guideline limits for particle exposure, above which health risks rise.

facts.text: For PM2.5 the annual mean should not exceed 5 μg/m3 and the 24-hour mean 15 μg/m3.
For PM10 the annual mean should not exceed 15 μg/m3 and the 24-hour mean 45 μg/m3.
Under the 2021 guideline, 97% of the world's population is exposed to unsafe PM2.5 levels.

definition.text: The burden of particle pollution falls more heavily on non-White people and those living in poverty.

facts.text: Living near particle-emitting facilities raises PM2.5 exposure and rates of illness and death.
In the US, disparities for Black people are larger than income alone explains, and scholars link them to housing segregation.
About 1.6 billion people live near sources of PM2.5 and other toxins, 900 million of them near super-emitting facilities.

definition.text: Aerosols change Earth's climate by altering how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat the planet keeps.

facts.text: They act directly, by scattering and absorbing radiation, and indirectly, by changing clouds, since cloud droplets form on particles.
The direct effect produces a net negative radiative forcing, that is, cooling.
Aerosol effects are the biggest source of uncertainty in climate predictions.
Soot is a strong absorber of radiation, while sea-salt particles only scatter it.

definition.text: Industries control particle emissions with dust collection systems such as cyclones, fabric filters, wet scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators.

facts.text: Particle emissions are highly regulated in most industrialised countries.
Fabric filters, or baghouses, are the most common in general industry.
Electrostatic precipitators charge particles and collect them on large charged plates.
